chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
title: Gunable's mouthpiece exercises for tone
summary: Gunable, a top East Coast teacher, had pupils build embouchure strength by blowing the mouthpiece alone, which McRae credits for his tone.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Who were some of your musical compatriots in Philadelphia who may be known by the jazz public as well as relatively unknown? People who you may have played with or studied with?
Well, the fellow I just -- I don't know if anybody know this fellow's name, Mike Gunable. He was one of the top teachers in the East.
And really, though, I think he came from St. Louis. Somebody recommended me to him as a teacher. And he really turned me out. He was really a fine teacher.
He give you things to do. He'll tell you to come to practice on a Sunday, and leave your horn -- don't bring your horn. Just bring your

And this way, he would strengthen up your muscles and your -- you know, the lower part of your neck so you don't move your mouthpiece around when you're playing. You don't stick your jaw out, you don't develop a lot of wind. It developes the muscles so your face will look the same way when you're blowing.
In other words, you had your --

Yeah, just hold your mouthpiece and just blow in it. That would develop your tone. This was very important. This was one of the things that I think that gave me the tone and technique (inaudible) I had -- I was recommended for that.
Everybody thought I had a beautiful tone and my technique. So --
